Require producer-stamped causal links alongside offset checks: the links caught four contiguous-offset misses, while detection of 30 noncontiguous gaps was retained. The decision selects the combined checks without extending those findings to unreported recovery or performance outcomes.

I propose quorum-published causal-frontier manifests, pipelined incremental state transfer, broker-log replay, and lease-fenced transactional sink epochs for recoverable snapshots of migrating stream operators. How do these pieces fit together?

The causal-frontier manifest would describe a recovery boundary; quorum publication is intended to make that boundary reliably available and unambiguous. Pipelined incremental state transfer addresses moving operator state while processing continues. Broker-log replay provides a way to account for records not represented in the selected state. Lease-fenced transactional sink epochs address which owner can make outputs visible during and after migration. Together, these are a proposed architecture, not a demonstrated recovery or performance result.
What does a causal frontier add to a snapshot manifest?

It makes the boundary about logical progress, not merely the time at which some state was copied. For a consistent cut, the state and records selected for recovery must respect causal prerequisites: the effect of a record cannot be included while a required predecessor is unaccounted for. The proposal does not specify the manifest's representation or how the frontier is calculated.
Is a manifest just a list of state files?

Not necessarily. In this proposal, its defining role is to identify a causal frontier for recovery. It would have to relate the selected state to the relevant recorded progress, but the proposal does not define its fields or storage layout. Calling it only a file list would leave that causal-boundary role unexplained.
Why publish the manifest through a quorum?

The intended benefit is that recovery and migration do not depend on one worker's private, possibly lost account of the frontier. Quorum publication suggests that a boundary becomes usable only when its publication meets a specified agreement condition. The proposal does not say how many participants form the quorum, where they reside, or how publication is implemented.
Does quorum-published mean every worker pauses until the manifest is published?

No such pause is specified. Quorum publication describes a condition on the manifest's availability or acceptance, not a requirement to stop processing globally. The architecture still has to meet the explicit constraint against global processing pauses; the term “quorum” alone does not establish that it does.
If publication is still under way when a worker crashes, which frontier does recovery use?

That selection rule is not given. Recovery would need an unambiguous, usable published boundary rather than treating a partially published frontier as unquestionably valid. The proposal names quorum publication as the intended foundation but does not specify what recovery selects at each possible crash timing.
Could the state chosen by the manifest and the broker log disagree?

They could unless the design connects them carefully. Broker-log replay should account for effects missing from the state selected at the frontier, not indiscriminately apply records whose effects are already represented there. Conversely, an effect absent from the state cannot be silently excluded from recoverable records if the cut requires it.
Does finding a record in the broker log prove it needs replay?

No. The broker log makes a record available, but availability is different from whether its effect is missing at the selected causal frontier. Recovery must interpret the log relative to the manifest and recovered state. The proposal does not prescribe the record-by-record replay rule.
What if messages arrive reordered across channels?

Reordering is part of the setting the proposal must handle. A record's arrival position cannot, by itself, determine whether it belongs before or after the recoverable causal frontier. The frontier and broker-log interpretation need to account for causal prerequisites even when their records arrive in an inconvenient order.
Does a causal frontier impose one total order on all messages?

Not by its name. It describes a logically coherent boundary; that is different from requiring a new total order of every record across the distributed stream. The proposal does not specify an ordering scheme or a rule that eliminates reordering.
Why is the state transfer both pipelined and incremental?

“Incremental” proposes transferring state in portions rather than treating the entire state as one indivisible transfer. “Pipelined” proposes allowing transfer work to overlap with other work instead of necessarily waiting for every portion to finish before continuing. Those choices are relevant to migration without a global processing pause, but no transfer schedule or measured overhead is stated.
Can a partially transferred state be treated as a complete snapshot?

Not merely because some portions have arrived. The recovery boundary must identify a coherent state view, regardless of how transfer is pipelined. If migration or a crash occurs mid-transfer, recovery needs a way to distinguish usable transferred state from an incomplete transfer. The proposal does not specify how it makes that distinction.
Is pipelined transfer itself the recovery mechanism?

No. It concerns moving state during migration. The causal-frontier manifest and broker-log replay address the recovery view, and lease-fenced transactional sink epochs address output visibility. All four need compatible boundaries; transfer alone would not establish a consistent cut or exactly-once outputs.
What is the role of a lease in the sink epochs?

Lease fencing is intended to keep activity from an owner without current authority from making a conflicting sink commit. The transactional epoch gives commits an execution context that can be distinguished across an ownership change. The proposal does not specify lease duration, epoch assignment, or the sink's precise fencing and transaction protocol.
Can an old owner keep processing records after its lease is fenced?

The safety question is whether any such activity can count as authoritative, particularly at the sink. Lease fencing is proposed to exclude conflicting commits across ownership changes. It does not, by itself, claim that every internal operation by an old owner physically stops at the same instant.
Does a transactional sink epoch determine which broker records belong in the snapshot?

No. The causal-frontier manifest and its relationship to state and the broker log determine the recovery boundary. Sink epochs concern output commits under changing authority. The boundaries must agree in a correct design, but the epoch is not a substitute for choosing a consistent cut.
Could a recovered cut be consistent while outputs are committed twice?

Conceptually, yes. A coherent internal cut does not alone tell recovery whether an output was already committed before a crash. Lease-fenced transactional sink epochs are proposed to address that separate visibility issue. The proposal has not yet established that they do so.
Could sink commits be unique while the recovered cut is inconsistent?

Yes. Preventing a second visible commit does not repair a recovered state that omits a causal predecessor or double-applies a logged record. Both a consistent cut and exactly-once outputs are required after any single worker crash.
Does “transactional” alone prove exactly-once outputs?

No. A transaction governs a commit boundary, but recovery must also know how committed effects relate to replayed inputs and the selected frontier. The proposal provides no complete sink protocol or evidence that it prevents both duplicates and omissions after a crash.
How do these components interact when an operator migrates during a snapshot?

The published frontier would need to identify the state-and-record view recovery can use despite the move. Pipelined incremental transfer would need to preserve that view even if only part of the moving state has arrived. Broker-log replay would need to account for effects not included in that view, and sink fencing would need to prevent conflicting visible commits across ownership epochs. That describes the required interaction, not an implemented handoff sequence.
What if a worker crashes during that incremental transfer?

The design's explicit recovery target still applies to any single worker crash. A recoverable published frontier, usable state, and appropriate broker records would have to support a consistent cut without assuming the interrupted transfer finished. The proposal does not specify which transferred portions survive or the precise recovery steps.
The overall problem mentions concurrent worker failures. Does quorum publication make arbitrary simultaneous crashes safe?

That does not follow. Quorum publication is proposed as part of the recovery architecture, but its membership, placement, and failure tolerance are unspecified. The explicit guarantee to meet is a consistent cut and exactly-once outputs after any single worker crash; arbitrary concurrent-crash tolerance cannot be inferred.
Can I say the broker will always retain everything needed after a crash?

Not as an established fact. Broker-log replay depends on the needed records being available and correctly related to the published frontier, but the proposal does not state retention limits, durability rules, or a result showing that availability under every relevant crash.
How could a late causal predecessor complicate the proposed frontier?

If a record's effect appears in the recovered state or in work authorized to commit, but a predecessor required to justify it is absent from the selected view, the cut would be inconsistent. The fact that the predecessor arrives late does not remove the dependency. The frontier and replay interpretation have to account for it without assuming arrival order reflects causal order.
Does quorum publication guarantee the frontier itself is causally correct?

No. Publication can make a stated frontier reliably agreed upon without proving that the frontier accurately describes the state and records. Both the construction of a consistent frontier and its publication matter. The proposal names quorum publication but does not provide a correctness argument for the frontier's contents.
What does this proposal suggest about the no-global-pause requirement?

Pipelined incremental transfer and a published recovery boundary are compatible with processing continuing while migration and snapshot work proceed. But the proposal alone does not prove that quorum publication, replay preparation, or sink coordination avoids a global processing pause. That condition requires its own demonstration.
What about the numerical throughput target?

The design must maintain at least 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput. Incremental transfer, broker-log handling, manifest publication, and transactional commits could all affect that ratio. No throughput benchmark or result is included in this proposal, so meeting the 85% threshold cannot be asserted.
If we eventually saw throughput above 85%, would that establish there were no global pauses?

No. An aggregate throughput ratio cannot by itself rule out a global processing pause. The target has two parts: at least 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput and no global processing pause. Both would need to be addressed independently.
And if there were no global pauses, would performance automatically clear 85%?

No. Continuous processing could still incur enough ongoing publication, transfer, replay, or sink overhead to fall below the throughput threshold. Avoiding a global stop and meeting the relative throughput floor are distinct requirements.
Is this proposal a decision to adopt all four components now?

It is a proposal to use them together. It does not report implementation, select the architecture as a final decision, or present recovery and performance findings. Describing it as already adopted or validated would change its status.
What would be the core correctness question for the combined architecture?

Whether the quorum-published causal frontier consistently identifies recoverable state and broker-log effects through migration and a single worker crash, while lease-fenced sink epochs make each required output visible exactly once. That question includes the relationship among the components; none can establish the full guarantee in isolation.
Can you state the complete proposal briefly without turning the design goals into results?

Propose quorum-published causal-frontier manifests, pipelined incremental state transfer, broker-log replay, and lease-fenced transactional sink epochs for migrating stream operators. The design would still need to demonstrate a consistent cut and exactly-once outputs after any single worker crash, at least 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput, and no global processing pause.

That is an implementation and validation plan, not a set of completed results. The planned implementation concerns pipelined frontier manifests and fenced sinks. The validation then has three distinct subjects: recovered cuts under reordering and crashes, commit uniqueness, and MoveBench-64 throughput at or above 85% of the snapshot-disabled baseline without globally pausing processing.

It is meant to identify which state and recorded effects belong to the recovery point. The crash-cut validation must check that this view remains logically coherent when records reorder and a worker crashes. A manifest's existence alone would not establish that its frontier describes a consistent cut.
Can a recovered cut look coherent on one worker but still be inconsistent overall?

Yes. The cut is distributed. Individually plausible state views can disagree about whether a message's effect belongs in the recovered computation. The planned validation must examine their relationship, not merely whether each part can be read after a crash.
How does reordering affect what that validation needs to establish?

It prevents arrival order from serving as a reliable definition of the cut. A record can arrive late without its causal relationship changing. The validation needs to examine whether the recovered view accounts for required predecessors and record effects despite reordered delivery; the plan does not prescribe a particular test pattern or algorithm.
Should I call these tests an exhaustive proof for every crash timing?

No. The plan says to validate reordered crash cuts but provides no case count, timing schedule, or exhaustive-coverage claim. The overall recovery requirement is for any single worker crash; the planned validation is directed at that requirement, not itself a completed proof.
Does this plan specify simultaneous failures of multiple workers?

It does not specify a multi-worker crash test. The broader design setting includes concurrent worker failures, while the explicit recovery guarantee is a consistent cut and exactly-once outputs after any single worker crash. Do not add a simultaneous-failure test condition to this plan.
What are the fenced sinks supposed to protect?

They are intended to keep sink commits associated with valid authority as an operator migrates or recovery changes who may act. The plan calls for implementing them and validating unique commits; it does not define a fencing protocol or claim that conflicting commits have already been prevented.
Does “fenced” mean the former owner can never do any internal work?

Not necessarily. The important output-side question is which activity may produce a commit that counts. The plan does not specify how an old worker's internal execution is stopped or how fencing is enforced at the sink.
Why measure unique commits separately from recovered cuts?

The recovered cut concerns the internal recovery boundary. Commit uniqueness concerns what becomes durably visible at the sink. A consistent cut does not automatically prevent a repeated sink commit, and a uniqueness check does not automatically show the recovered cut is consistent.
If commits are unique, have we established exactly-once outputs?

Not on that finding alone. Uniqueness rules out duplicate commits, but exactly-once outputs also require that expected outputs are not omitted. This plan explicitly names unique-commit validation; it does not specify a separate output-completeness measurement.
Could an output be missed even when every observed commit is unique?

Yes. A set of commits can contain no duplicates while lacking an expected output. That is why the planned uniqueness check should be described by its actual scope rather than treated as the entire exactly-once guarantee.
Does the plan choose transaction identifiers for the sinks?
No. It calls for fenced sinks and a check of unique commits. It does not specify identifier formats, transaction boundaries, or how the sink recognizes a commit attempted after recovery.
Where does migration enter the cut and sink checks?

The frontier and sink authority must remain meaningful while a stream operator moves. Recovery cannot combine incompatible state and record views across that move, and a change of owner must not turn a repeated attempt into a second valid commit. Those are the concerns the planned checks address; no handoff sequence is specified here.
Does pipelining guarantee the implementation won't globally pause processing?

No. Pipelining is compatible with overlapping snapshot work and processing, but it does not prove that every step avoids a global pause. The plan explicitly calls for validating pause-free performance rather than assuming it from the design term.
What exactly should “pause-free” mean in this performance target?
In the context of the stated goal, it means without globally pausing processing. It does not imply that no individual worker can ever wait or that every operation has zero latency.
Could the benchmark clear 85% while still having a global processing pause?

An aggregate throughput ratio alone would not rule that out. The plan couples the throughput threshold with the requirement to be pause-free in the global sense; both observations need to be established separately.
And could there be no global pause but throughput below 85%?

Yes. Processing might continue everywhere while ongoing snapshot, transfer, or sink work still reduces throughput too much. Avoiding a global pause would not substitute for meeting the numerical floor.
Which throughput is the 85% compared with?
Throughput with snapshots disabled. The target for MoveBench-64 is at least 85% of that baseline, not 85% of another snapshot-enabled design's throughput and not an absolute rate.
If the snapshot-disabled baseline is expressed as 100%, what does the plan require?

It requires the measured MoveBench-64 throughput to be at least 85% on that scale, while processing is not globally paused. That permits up to a 15-percentage-point reduction relative to the snapshot-disabled baseline, but no measurement is reported by the plan.
Does naming MoveBench-64 supply its measured throughput?
No. It names the benchmark to use for validation. The plan provides the threshold, not a measured percentage for the planned implementation.
Should I bring a previously observed throughput percentage into this plan as though it were the result of pipelined frontier manifests?

No. This node specifies a future MoveBench-64 validation of the planned implementation. It does not report throughput for pipelined frontier manifests and fenced sinks, so assigning it a measurement from a different evaluation would add an unsupported result.
Does the plan define the number of crash tests or the degree of reordering?
No. It names reordered crash cuts as a validation subject but gives no crash count, reordering percentage, or particular record schedule. Those should not be supplied as if they were specified here.
What would be an overstatement of the implementation part?

Saying the manifests or fenced sinks are already running correctly would overstate it. The stated action is to implement them; the later checks are meant to assess their behavior. No implementation outcome has yet been reported.
And what would overstate the validation part?

Saying that reordered crash cuts have matched, commits were unique, or MoveBench-64 reached at least 85% without global pauses would turn planned checks into findings. The plan specifies what to validate, not what validation found.
If a throughput check succeeds but cuts fail under reordering, does that satisfy the plan's purpose?
No. The checks address separate necessary aspects of the design. Throughput at or above 85% cannot compensate for an inconsistent recovered cut after a crash.
If cuts look correct but commits are duplicated?
Then the planned unique-commit check would fail even if the cut check succeeded. Internal recovery consistency and sink-visible behavior must both be assessed.
And if cuts and commits pass but MoveBench-64 is below the floor?
The performance part would remain unmet. The plan calls for pause-free MoveBench-64 throughput of at least 85% of the snapshot-disabled baseline as well as the recovery and commit checks.
Can you give me a compact statement of the plan without implying that any check has passed?

Implement pipelined causal-frontier manifests and fenced sinks; then validate recovered cuts under reordered messages and crashes, unique commits, and MoveBench-64 throughput of at least 85% of the snapshot-disabled baseline without global processing pauses. These are planned implementation and validation steps, not reported outcomes.

I propose vector-frontier microbatch checkpoints with indexed causal-link validation, replicated incremental state, and epoch-fenced transactional sinks for migrating stream operators. How would these pieces fit together?

They address different boundaries of a recoverable snapshot. A vector frontier would describe the logical progress captured by each microbatch checkpoint. Indexed causal-link validation would check whether that proposed boundary accounts for required predecessors, even when messages reorder. Replicated incremental state would make the state associated with recovery available as operators migrate. Epoch-fenced transactional sinks would control which outputs can become visible across ownership changes and recovery. This is a proposal, not an implemented or measured result.
Why use a vector frontier rather than describe the checkpoint by one time?

A single wall-clock time does not, by itself, express which distributed message effects depend on which predecessors. A vector frontier is proposed to describe progress across components of the computation while retaining the relationships needed for a consistent cut. The proposal does not specify the vector's dimensions, encoding, or construction rule.
What does “microbatch” change about the checkpoint idea?

It says checkpoint work is organized around microbatches rather than described as one undifferentiated global capture. The frontier still has to identify a coherent recovery boundary across the distributed computation. The proposal gives no microbatch size, duration, or rule requiring all workers to finish a batch simultaneously.
So I shouldn't assume that a microbatch checkpoint requires stopping all operators together?

Correct. A global processing pause would conflict with the stated design constraint. Organizing checkpoints by microbatch does not automatically require such a pause, but it also does not prove that a particular implementation avoids one.
Could independently completed microbatches produce an inconsistent recovery view?

Yes, if their selected state and message effects do not fit one logical frontier. The checkpoint needs to account for causal prerequisites across those portions of the computation. Calling each portion a microbatch checkpoint does not alone establish a consistent distributed cut.
What does the causal-link validation actually need to check?

At a conceptual level, it must check whether effects admitted by the proposed vector frontier have their required causal predecessors accounted for. A record might arrive after another record yet still be a predecessor, especially across partitions or during migration. The proposal does not specify the precise validation algorithm or what information each link contains.
Why specify that the causal-link validation is indexed?

“Indexed” suggests that the links relevant to a frontier can be located for validation without treating them as an unstructured collection. Its intended role is to make causal checking practical alongside checkpointing. The proposal does not identify an index structure, build procedure, update cost, or measured speedup.
Does the index itself certify that the causal links are accurate?

No. An index helps find information; it does not prove that the information correctly represents a record's dependencies. For the validation to support a consistent cut, the links it examines must be meaningful and must be compared with the state and progress actually represented by the proposed frontier.
Can indexed validation infer all dependencies from contiguous broker offsets?

Offset contiguity alone does not establish cross-partition causal completeness. The proposed causal-link validation must examine the relevant dependency relationships, not equate consecutive offsets with proof that every predecessor has been incorporated. The proposal does not prescribe a broker-offset scheme for the index.
If validation finds an unmet predecessor, does the proposal specify what happens to the checkpoint?

No. It identifies indexed causal-link validation as a component, but does not choose whether the frontier is adjusted, checkpoint completion waits, or another action is taken. What is essential conceptually is not to treat an unaccounted-for predecessor as though it belongs to a consistent cut.
Does detecting a predecessor gap mean its record has already been recovered?

No. Detection identifies an effect that the recovery boundary may still need to account for. Availability and replay of that effect are separate matters. This proposal does not provide a record-level replay procedure.
Where does replicated incremental state fit in?

It supplies the state side of the proposed recovery approach. “Incremental” indicates state can be maintained or transferred in portions rather than as an indivisible full copy, while “replicated” indicates the design is not meant to rely solely on one worker's local state surviving. The proposal does not specify replica count, placement, or how incremental updates become recoverable.
Can I say every replica necessarily contains a complete current state at every instant?

No. That would add a synchronization property not stated here. The relevant question is whether recovery can assemble a usable state corresponding to the selected vector-frontier checkpoint after a worker crash. Merely naming replicated incremental state does not establish that every replica is immediately current.
What happens if migration is in progress when a worker crashes?

The recovered frontier, the available replicated state, and the authority to commit outputs would have to describe one coherent continuation despite the interrupted move. The proposal is meant for migrating operators, but it does not specify a migration handoff sequence or identify which state portion is selected at each crash timing.
Does replication make the vector frontier consistent automatically?

No. Replication concerns the availability of state, while consistency concerns whether that state, its recorded message effects, and the proposed frontier agree. Replicas could be available without establishing which combination constitutes a valid cut.
If messages are reordered, can we assign each one to a checkpoint just by when it arrives?

Not safely on arrival timing alone. Reordering means a message's causal role can differ from what its arrival position suggests. The vector frontier and causal-link check have to provide a coherent interpretation of which effects the recoverable checkpoint represents.
What is the “epoch-fenced” part of the sink proposal protecting?

It is intended to keep sink commits from conflicting execution or ownership epochs from both counting during migration and recovery. An owner that is no longer authorized should not be able to create a competing visible commit. The proposal does not specify how epochs are assigned or how the sink enforces the fence.
And why do the sinks need to be transactional as well?

Transactionality concerns when a group of output effects becomes committed and visible. Fencing concerns which epoch is authorized to commit. Combining them is intended to prevent recovery or an overlapping owner from making a previously committed output visible again, but the proposal does not specify transaction boundaries or provide an exactly-once proof.
Is epoch fencing a replacement for validating the causal frontier?

No. Fencing protects commit authority; causal validation protects the logical recovery boundary. A uniquely authorized owner could still use an inconsistent checkpoint, and a consistent checkpoint alone would not settle whether an output was already committed. Both concerns have to be addressed.
Could commits be unique while expected outputs are missing?

Yes. No duplicate commits would establish only uniqueness, not completeness. The stated goal is exactly-once outputs after any single worker crash, which requires avoiding both repeated and omitted visible effects. The proposed transactional sinks must work coherently with the recovered cut to meet that goal.
Does this proposal promise recovery from arbitrary simultaneous worker crashes?

No. Concurrent worker failures are part of the broader setting, but the explicit recovery guarantee to meet is a consistent cut and exactly-once outputs after any single worker crash. The proposal gives no replica placement or failure-tolerance argument that would justify a guarantee for arbitrary simultaneous failures.
Could a crash of any one worker be relevant, or only the current operator owner?

The goal says any single worker crash, so the guarantee cannot silently be restricted to a designated owner. The proposal would need a recovery account for the relevant worker roles, without claiming a particular role-specific procedure has already been defined.
How do the frontier and sink epochs need to agree?

Recovery must not replay an effect against a selected frontier and then commit its output a second time merely because ownership moved to another epoch. Conversely, an effect required by the recovered view must not disappear at the sink. The proposal needs a coherent relationship between the recovery boundary and the sink's commit boundary; it does not spell out that relationship.
Does the microbatch checkpoint automatically determine which sink transaction is committed?

Not from the proposal as stated. A checkpoint boundary and a sink transaction boundary are distinct. To support exactly-once outputs, an implementation would need to relate them consistently, but no correspondence or commit rule is specified here.
What is the throughput requirement this architecture would need to satisfy?

It must maintain at least 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput without globally pausing processing. That 85% is relative to the throughput baseline with snapshots disabled, not to another snapshot-enabled configuration or a fixed number of records per second.
Could indexing and incremental replication help with that performance goal?

They are plausible ways to organize validation and state movement without treating every checkpoint as a full, globally stopped operation. But they also introduce work. The proposal contains no benchmark or measurement showing whether their combined cost meets the 85% floor.
Would achieving 85% by pausing every worker briefly meet the goal?

No. The throughput floor and the prohibition on globally pausing processing are separate requirements. Meeting exactly 85% of the snapshot-disabled baseline would satisfy the numerical threshold, but not excuse a global processing pause.
Would having no global pause prove throughput is high enough?

No. Index maintenance, validation, replication, and sink transactions could impose ongoing overhead even if processing continues everywhere. The throughput comparison would still have to reach at least 85% of the snapshot-disabled baseline.
Do we know a microbatch duration or an index lookup cost for this proposal?
No. Neither a microbatch duration nor a measured index cost is specified. Assigning either a number would turn this conceptual proposal into an invented configuration or result.
Can you state the unresolved correctness interface in one place?

The selected vector frontier must agree with the replicated incremental state and with the causal links checked by the index, even as messages reorder and operators migrate. Recovery must then agree with epoch-fenced transactional sink commits about which output effects are already visible. The proposal names these interfaces but does not give the protocol that makes them correct.
Give me a concise formulation that remains a proposal rather than a claim of success.

Propose vector-frontier microbatch checkpoints with indexed causal-link validation, replicated incremental state, and epoch-fenced transactional sinks. The design still needs to demonstrate a consistent cut and exactly-once outputs after any single worker crash, plus at least 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput without globally pausing processing.
Can indexed causal-link checks skip per-record lookups without missing stale-vector predecessors at microbatch boundaries?

That is an open correctness-versus-work question for vector-frontier microbatch checkpoints. An index might let validation avoid examining each record separately, but skipping a lookup is safe only if the information consulted still reveals every predecessor that matters to the boundary—even when a record's dependency vector is stale. No such safe skipping rule is specified yet.
What exactly would we be skipping?

The proposed shortcut is to avoid an individual causal-link lookup for some records. It does not mean that their causal requirements cease to matter. The unresolved issue is whether an indexed check can establish those requirements without consulting each record's link individually.
Why do microbatch boundaries make that question harder?

A boundary determines which effects are treated as already represented in a checkpoint and which remain to be accounted for. A predecessor associated with a record near that boundary can matter even if the record is handled in another microbatch or arrives out of order. Skipping a check must not make that predecessor disappear from the frontier's interpretation.
Could we simply trust each record's attached dependency vector to summarize its predecessors?

That would not answer the stale-vector part of the question. If an attached vector is stale, consulting it—or treating an indexed summary of it as complete—might overlook a required predecessor. A safe shortcut needs an account of causal dependencies that remains reliable in precisely that case.
Is a stale vector necessarily evidence that its predecessor is absent from the checkpoint?

No. Staleness concerns the accuracy of the vector's description of dependencies. Whether a particular predecessor is already included in the selected state is a separate question. Validation has to distinguish a missing requirement from a requirement whose effect is already accounted for.
If the broker offsets are contiguous at the boundary, can the index skip the link checks?

Offset contiguity alone is not proof of cross-partition causal completeness. A predecessor requirement can go unrepresented by stale vector information while offsets appear contiguous. The question asks whether an index can safely skip per-record work without depending on that insufficient inference.
What would an index need to represent in principle?

It would need to preserve enough information about the causal requirements relevant to a proposed microbatch frontier to decide whether any required predecessor is unaccounted for. An index that summarizes only observed offset continuity, or only dependency vectors assumed to be current, would not by its name solve the stale-vector concern. No particular index structure has been selected.
Could an aggregate entry for a whole microbatch replace every individual lookup?

Possibly, but only if that entry faithfully covers the dependencies that matter at the boundary, including those associated with stale-vector records. The proposal does not establish that such an aggregate exists or specify how its coverage would be demonstrated. An aggregate cannot be presumed complete merely because it is indexed.
Is the key test whether there are no gaps anywhere in the batch?

More precisely, it is whether the proposed checkpoint frontier accounts for the causal predecessors required by effects it includes. A gap associated with a record at the boundary could matter even if other records in the microbatch are accounted for. The test cannot silently equate a batch-level progress marker with every record's causal completeness.
How does reordering affect the shortcut?

Reordering means arrival position is not a reliable proxy for causal position. A record that arrives later can carry a requirement relevant to an earlier-looking frontier, and a record already seen need not have every predecessor accounted for. An indexed shortcut must preserve the relevant dependency information independently of convenient arrival order.
Does a causal-link lookup mean replaying the predecessor?

No. A lookup concerns discovering or checking a causal relationship. Detecting an unmet predecessor and obtaining or applying its effect are distinct tasks. This question is about reducing lookup work without losing detection, not about specifying replay.
Would scanning every record be the straightforward comparison point conceptually?

It is a useful conceptual contrast: per-record lookups consult each relevant record separately, whereas the proposed indexed check hopes to avoid some of that work. That contrast does not establish that a full scan is the chosen design or give a measured cost for either method.
Does skipping per-record lookups necessarily improve throughput?

Not necessarily. An index can have maintenance and query costs of its own. The motivation is to reduce validation work, but the question states no throughput measurement or guarantee that a shortcut will improve performance, let alone meet the at-least-85% snapshot-disabled throughput goal.
Could an indexed check return ‘complete’ for a microbatch and still miss a predecessor?

Yes, if its notion of completeness omits a causal link needed at the boundary—for example, because it relies on stale dependency information. That possibility is what the question is probing. ‘Complete’ must have a justified relationship to the actual causal requirements, not just to what was convenient to index.
What about a predecessor that belongs to a different partition from the boundary record?

That cross-partition relationship must still be accounted for. A microbatch or index organized around one partition cannot assume its local progress describes every predecessor elsewhere. The question supplies no cross-partition indexing rule, so whether such a relationship can be checked without the per-record lookup remains open.
Could the index be checked once when each microbatch ends?

That is a possible shape for a check, but no timing rule is given. To answer the question, one would have to show that whatever check is made at the boundary covers the relevant records and predecessors before that frontier is treated as recoverable. Checking once is not inherently safe or unsafe without that coverage argument.
If a buffered record moves during migration, does its index entry automatically move with it?

Nothing in the question establishes that. Migration could affect where a buffered record and its causal information are visible, so a sound shortcut would need to account for those records at the microbatch boundary. The design has not specified how index entries are maintained through migration.
Is the concern that promotion might trust an incomplete indexed view?

That is one way to frame it. If an indexed check omits a buffered record's required predecessor, a promoted owner might treat the microbatch frontier as complete on incomplete information. The question asks whether skipping per-record lookups can be made safe against that possibility; it does not assert that such a promotion has occurred.
Could the sink's epoch fence compensate if the index misses a causal predecessor?

No. Epoch fencing addresses which owner is authorized to commit outputs. It does not reveal a predecessor absent from the chosen recovery cut. Commit authority and causal completeness are separate requirements.
Could unique commits nevertheless coexist with a missed predecessor?

Yes, conceptually. An output may not be duplicated even though the state-and-message view omits a required causal predecessor. A safe indexed shortcut therefore needs its own cut-consistency argument; sink uniqueness would not establish it.
Do we need to prove the shortcut detects every stale-vector predecessor, or only most of them?

The question is explicitly whether it can skip per-record lookups *without missing* stale-vector predecessors at microbatch boundaries. An approach that sometimes misses one would not answer that question affirmatively. No statistical tolerance or permitted miss rate is stated.
Could we decide to check every record with a stale vector and skip the others?

That would require a reliable way to recognize which vectors are stale before making the decision to skip. The question does not supply such a test. Labeling only known-stale records for individual checks would not establish safety if some stale vectors remain unidentified.
Would a record's position below a checkpointed offset make its dependency vector trustworthy?

No such implication is stated. An offset position describes broker progress, while vector accuracy concerns the record's expressed causal relationships. A safe indexed check cannot assume one proves the other.
What would a convincing evaluation compare?

It would compare the predecessors the indexed check identifies at microbatch boundaries with an independent account of the predecessors actually required, paying particular attention to stale-vector records and any lookups skipped. Performance could then be measured separately. That describes the evidence needed to answer the question, not a test already run or a chosen oracle or benchmark configuration.
Would finding no missed predecessors in a finite run prove the shortcut safe for every migration?

No. It would be evidence within the conditions tested, not a universal proof across all reorderings, migrations, and crash timings. A broader safety claim would also need an argument that the index's coverage cannot omit a boundary-relevant dependency.
Does this question already select an index design or a microbatch size?

No. It asks whether indexed causal-link checks can avoid per-record lookups safely. It specifies neither the index representation nor a microbatch size, lookup policy, update procedure, or performance result.
Can you state the unresolved tradeoff in one sentence?

Can an indexed check reduce per-record causal-link lookups at vector-frontier microbatch boundaries while still exposing every predecessor concealed by a stale dependency vector before the boundary is accepted as a recoverable cut?

My hypothesis is that partition-level causal-link interval indexes can validate microbatch frontier ranges without per-record lookups, detect all four CausalGap-2k misses, and sustain at least 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput.

That proposes both a correctness outcome and a performance outcome. The indexes would support validation of microbatch frontier ranges without looking up each record individually. The specific detection prediction is all four CausalGap-2k misses; the performance prediction is throughput of at least 85% of the snapshot-disabled baseline. Neither outcome is established by the hypothesis.
What does “partition-level” specify about the proposed index?

It places the index at the granularity of a partition, rather than describing a separate lookup for each record being validated. It does not specify the number of partitions, where the indexes live, or how entries are maintained.
Why call it a causal-link interval index instead of an offset index?

The intended information concerns causal links associated with intervals, not just whether broker offsets are consecutive. An offset range can appear complete while a cross-partition predecessor remains unaccounted for. The hypothesis needs the index to expose that causal requirement when validating a frontier range; it does not define an index representation.
Does “interval” specify a fixed time window?
